name: Lincoln Rackhouse

profile.address: Meridian Parkway, Meridian Business Campus, Aurora, Naperville Township, DuPage County, Illinois, 60598
profile.reading:
This building at 4267 Meridian Parkway in Aurora, Illinois -- tagged in this record under the name "Lincoln Rackhouse" -- has changed hands since that name was attached to it. The roughly 70,000-square-foot facility, with about 33,000 square feet of technical white space, was originally built around 2007 for CNA Insurance's own data processing needs before being converted to a multi-tenant data center. It later passed through ownership by Bytegrid and Lincoln Rackhouse, a data-center investment and operating platform, before being acquired by Michigan-based colocation and cloud provider US Signal, as reported by trade press covering the deal. At acquisition, the facility was reported to have about 1.35 megawatts of IT capacity in active use against a planned build-out toward 4 megawatts of critical capacity (roughly 6 megawatts of commercial/utility power), giving US Signal substantial room to grow into the space as demand increased.

Lincoln Rackhouse itself was a real estate and data-center operating arm associated with Lincoln Property Company, one of the larger private real estate investment and development firms in the United States, active in acquiring and repositioning data center assets for institutional ownership. Its presence in this building's history reflects a common pattern in the data center industry: purpose-built or converted facilities frequently change operators and brands as investment platforms buy, reposition, and resell them to operating companies better positioned to fill them with tenants.

For prospective and current customers, the facility today functions as a Chicago-area colocation site for US Signal rather than as an active Lincoln Rackhouse property, and readers should not expect to find current marketing, pricing, or capacity information under the Lincoln Rackhouse name. The Aurora location places it in the western Chicago suburbs, within reach of the Chicago metro's substantial enterprise and financial-services customer base while avoiding the highest real estate costs of the city core. No additional zoning, permit, or expansion filings specific to the post-acquisition period under US Signal were identified in public reporting. US Signal, the current operator, is a Michigan-based provider of colocation, cloud, and network services aimed primarily at midwestern enterprise and public-sector customers, and the Aurora building fits a pattern common to that segment of the industry: rather than building new facilities from the ground up, regional colocation providers frequently expand their geographic footprint by acquiring existing, already-powered buildings with room to grow, since the electrical infrastructure, generator plant, and physical security systems already in place represent most of a data center's upfront cost and lead time. That the site was originally built for a single insurance company's internal computing needs before being converted for multi-tenant use is itself a common origin story in the industry -- many of the colocation facilities operating today began as corporate-owned data centers that were later repurposed once their original occupants outgrew them, consolidated elsewhere, or moved workloads to the cloud.

profile.reading:
Lincoln Rackhouse Maryland is a data center at 12401 Prosperity Drive in Silver Spring, Maryland, roughly fifteen miles north of Washington, D.C. The facility sits on about fifteen acres and occupies a single story building of 214,000 square feet, split between 90,000 square feet of raised technical floor and 37,000 square feet of office and flex space. According to the operator's own materials, the building can support up to 4.7 megawatts of critical IT load, with roughly 2 megawatts available for new customers at the time the page was published. Power arrives on dual feeds from diverse 25kV substations, and standby power is provided by ten 2.25 megawatt diesel generators arranged in an N plus one configuration, backed by twenty eight 750 kVA uninterruptible power supply units. The site is built to support N plus one, N plus two, or fully redundant two N configurations depending on a customer's requirements.

Cooling is handled by two high temperature chilled water central plants that the operator describes as fully mechanically redundant, supported by a 135,000 gallon thermal storage tank and 315,000 gallons of makeup water storage, a setup meant to keep cooling running through a utility interruption without immediately depending on generators. Fire protection uses a dual pre-action dry pipe system, which is common in raised floor data halls because it reduces the risk of accidental water discharge near electronic equipment.

The building is marketed as carrier neutral, with more than twenty metro carriers available and named Tier 1 providers including AT&T, Comcast, Zayo, Lumen, and Verizon connecting on site through two separate meet me rooms. Physical security includes twenty four hour staffed guarding, a K-4 rated crash resistant perimeter fence, biometric access readers, and continuous video surveillance, and the operator describes the facility as built to Tier III standards.

The property is operated by Lincoln Rackhouse, the data center investment and development arm of Lincoln Property Company, a large national commercial real estate firm. That parentage is typical of the Rackhouse portfolio, which leases wholesale and colocation space in existing large format buildings rather than building single tenant campuses from scratch. Beyond the specifications published on the operator's own site, no additional detail on the building's construction date, prior use, or current tenant roster is publicly available, which is standard practice for a wholesale colocation asset where tenant identities are typically confidential.

reading:
Lincoln Rackhouse is the data centre arm of Lincoln Property Company, the Dallas based diversified real estate services firm. It was formed in September 2010 when Lincoln acquired the Rackhouse Group, a Dallas data centre tenant representation business founded in 2006 by the former Trammell Crow executives Martin Peck, Peter Tippen and Brant Bernet, and the combined business subsequently expanded from tenant representation into development, ownership and facilities management. That mixed model, part landlord and part service provider, distinguishes it from the wholesale developers and colocation REITs elsewhere in this registry.

The Maryland facility is well documented by the operator. It sits at 12401 Prosperity Drive in Silver Spring, Maryland, about 15 miles north of Washington DC, on a 15 acre site, in a 214,000 square foot single storey existing building containing 90,000 square feet of raised floor and 37,000 square feet of office and flex space. The power figures are published separately and should stay separate. Critical IT load available is stated as 4.7 MW, sitting within 7.2 MW of concurrently maintainable infrastructure, with 2 MW described as currently available. Utility service is dual fed by two 25 kV lines from diverse substations. Standby generation is ten generators of 2.25 MW each in an N plus one arrangement, and the uninterruptible supply comprises 28 units of 750 kVA. Cooling runs on two high temperature chilled water central plants offering full mechanical redundancy, with 135,000 gallons of thermal storage and 315,000 gallons of makeup storage. More than 20 metro carriers are available, with AT and T, Comcast, Zayo, Lumen and Verizon named, across two diverse meet me rooms, and the site has continuously staffed security and a K-4 rated perimeter fence. The 4.7 MW figure this registry holds for the facility is the operator's stated critical IT load, which is the correct measure to record.

A second facility row filed under this operator does not belong to it. The row covers a building in DuPage County, Illinois. The DuPage County assessment parcel at that location, PIN 0716303001 covering 5.25 acres, gives the property address as 4267 Meridian Parkway, Aurora, Illinois 60504, and names the owner as US Signal Prop Aurora LLC, billing to Grand Rapids, Michigan. US Signal's own site lists that exact address as its IL02 Aurora data centre, built in 2007, with a 4,000 kVA utility feed, a 4,000 kW generator plant in N plus one, 1,350 kW of uninterruptible supply expandable to 3 MW in a 2N configuration, 500 tons of cooling and five on net carriers.

The provenance of the error is visible in the map history. The Aurora polygon was drawn on 1 August 2011 as a plain building with no name. On 22 December 2024 a contributor added the name Lincoln Rackhouse and a data centre telecom tag in a changeset commented as adding a data centre to the map for a MapRoulette task, sourced to satellite imagery, with no operator tag, no address and no survey. The name came from a remote task list rather than from the ground. Lincoln Rackhouse's own portfolio lists no Illinois or Chicago area site at all, naming Plano, Texas alongside Maryland. The correct reading is one Lincoln Rackhouse facility here, in Maryland, and one Illinois row that belongs to US Signal.
